passage:
Dear Madhuri didi,
I need to tell someone, and you're the only one who won't laugh.
At lunch the girls in my group were making fun of the new boy's accent. Kritika did an imitation and everyone cracked up. I laughed too. I didn't think it was funny at all. I felt sick. He was sitting two tables away.
Then they asked if the school trip should be to the water park instead of the science museum. I actually really wanted the museum. I said, "Water park, obviously."
I keep doing this. I agree with whatever they say and laugh at whatever they laugh at, because if I don't, what if they stop saving me a seat?
Is this normal? It doesn't feel like me.
Love,
Vandana

qa.q: What did Vandana say about the school trip?
qa.a: Vandana said, "Water park, obviously," despite really wanting the museum.

qa.q: What is Vandana afraid will happen if Vandana disagrees with the group?
qa.a: Vandana fears they will stop saving a seat, so fitting in feels more important than honest opinions or feelings.

qa.q: What small step could Vandana try with the group?
qa.a: Vandana could start with something low-risk, like saying 'I'd actually like the museum', and notice whether real friends stay.

qa.q: How might the new boy feel if he heard the laughter?
qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and isolated, with no idea that at least one person laughing felt sick about it.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager admits laughing at disliked jokes and agreeing against a personal view out of fear of losing the group.

passage: Okay, so the topic this week is "times you weren't yourself." I'm Anjali, Class 12, and mine is basically all of Class 10. My group, Joseph, Nikhil and the others, had strong opinions on everything. If Joseph said a film was rubbish, I said it was rubbish, even though I'd loved it. When Nikhil made jokes about girls who "try too hard" in class, I laughed, and then I'd go home and do my homework in secret, because I was a girl who tried hard. The worst part was that I believed I had no choice. If I disagreed, maybe they'd drop me. It took a whole year, and one friend outside the group, before I tried saying "I actually liked it" about a film. Joseph shrugged and said, "Fair." That was it.

qa.q: What did Joseph say when Anjali finally said 'I actually liked it'?
qa.a: Joseph shrugged and said, "Fair."

qa.q: Why did Anjali laugh at Nikhil's jokes and then do homework in secret?
qa.a: She feared being dropped by the group, so she hid the part of herself that tried hard in class, even though the jokes hurt.

qa.q: What turning point does Anjali describe, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Saying 'I actually liked it' about a film was a small, safe test; Joseph's easy 'Fair' showed disagreeing didn't mean losing friends.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen Anjali's year of agreeing?
qa.a: Joseph may never have noticed, or may have assumed she truly agreed, which shows how much of the pressure lived in Anjali's fear.

grounding: On a school podcast, a teenager recalls a year of agreeing with friends and laughing at hurtful jokes out of fear of rejection.

passage: I'm Preeti, and I've known Jagdish since Class 3. On his own he's the kindest person, the kind who helps the watchman's son with maths after school. But around the cricket boys he's different. Yesterday at the bus stop, one of them made a joke about the watchman's son's torn shoes. Everyone laughed. Jagdish laughed too, a beat late, and then looked at the ground. When they said the new rule about phones in class was "dumb", Jagdish agreed loudly, even though last week he told me he thought it was fair. I don't know what he really thinks anymore. I don't think he knows either. He just watches their faces before he speaks.

qa.q: What did one of the cricket boys joke about at the bus stop?
qa.a: The watchman's son's torn shoes.

qa.q: What does Jagdish laughing 'a beat late' and looking at the ground suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he didn't find the joke funny and felt uneasy, but laughed so he wouldn't stand out from the group.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try the next time the group mocks someone?
qa.a: He could stay quiet instead of laughing, or say 'Leave it, yaar', and find that one small step doesn't have to cost him the group.

qa.q: How might the watchman's son feel if he knew Jagdish laughed?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and confused, since Jagdish is the one who helps him with maths after school.

grounding: A longtime friend watches a teenage boy laugh at jokes he dislikes and echo the group against his own view.

passage:
Monday: At lunch, Baljeet's group was mocking the new boy's accent. Lokesh didn't find it funny; his own cousin talked just like that. He laughed anyway, loudest of all, and checked Baljeet's face to see if it had been enough.
Wednesday: The group decided the school play was 'for losers'. Lokesh had secretly signed up. When Baljeet asked, 'You're not doing that, right?' he said, 'Obviously not,' and crossed his name off the list after school. His stomach hurt all evening.
Saturday: At the cricket ground, Baljeet made another joke about the new boy, Aniket, who was fielding nearby. Lokesh laughed on cue. Then he saw Aniket's face. Lokesh stopped laughing. He didn't say anything. But he didn't laugh again, and he noticed he could breathe a little easier.

qa.q: What did Lokesh cross off after school on Wednesday?
qa.a: His name, from the school play list.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh laugh loudest at a joke he didn't find funny?
qa.a: He feared being left out of Baljeet's group; laughing loudly and checking Baljeet's face was a way to prove he belonged, even against his own feelings.

qa.q: What was the small turning point on Saturday, and what could Lokesh do next?
qa.a: Seeing Aniket's face and stopping laughing; next, Lokesh could put his name back on the play list or quietly say hello to Aniket, choosing his own view over the group's.

qa.q: What might Aniket notice when Lokesh stops laughing?
qa.a: Aniket may notice that at least one person in the group isn't joining in, a small sign that he isn't completely alone.

grounding: A teenager laughs at jokes he dislikes and drops a play he wanted because the group's approval feels more important than his own view.

passage:
Karthik, I saw you nodding along when your friends said that thing about the girl in your class. You didn't look like you agreed. Let me tell you something from my school days.
At fifteen, in Mangaluru, I was in the group everyone wanted to be in. To stay in, I agreed with everything. They said the science fair was nerdy, so I said it too, though I loved it. They made fun of Reshma's weight, and I laughed, and then I went home and felt sick.
The worst part was that I stopped knowing what I actually thought. I'd wait to hear what they said first.
One day Reshma asked me, 'Sabina, do you even have your own opinion?' I had no answer.
It took me years to get my own voice back, beta. Don't hand yours over so cheaply.

qa.q: What did young Sabina's group say about the science fair?
qa.a: That it was nerdy.

qa.q: Why did young Sabina laugh at the jokes about Reshma and then feel sick?
qa.a: Sabina feared losing a place in the group, so laughed along; but it went against Sabina's own feelings, which came out as guilt at home.

qa.q: What choice is Sabina hoping Karthik will make?
qa.a: To stop nodding along when Karthik disagrees and to hold on to Karthik's own view even if the group frowns, before losing track of it.

qa.q: What might Reshma's question have been like from Reshma's side?
qa.a: Reshma, the target of the jokes, may have been hurt and frustrated, wanting to know whether Sabina really believed them or was only following.

grounding: An elder recalls agreeing with a popular group against their own view and laughing at cruel jokes out of fear of rejection.
